A crevasse is a deep crack in a glacier or a large body of ice.

That's the heart of it — but let's unpack every layer of that so the word truly sticks.

It is a crack — but not just any crack

A crevasse isn't a small scratch or a hairline fracture. It is a large, deep split — sometimes as deep as 45 metres (about 150 feet) or more — that cuts down through a glacier from the surface. The walls on either side of a crevasse are sheer faces of solid ice, and the gap between them can range from a narrow slit you could almost step over to a yawning chasm wide enough to swallow a bus.

It only forms in ice

This is the most important thing to remember. The word "crevasse" is specifically tied to glaciers and ice sheets. You would not call a crack in a rock, a wall, or the ground a crevasse. Those are called crevices or cracks. A crevasse belongs to the world of ice — glaciers, ice caps, and ice sheets like those in Antarctica or Greenland.

Why does ice crack?

A glacier is not a still, frozen block. It moves — slowly, but constantly — sliding downhill under its own enormous weight, like a river of ice. As it moves, different parts of the glacier flow at slightly different speeds. The surface ice is more rigid, while the deeper ice is under so much pressure that it behaves more like a thick, slow-moving paste. This difference in flow creates tension and stress in the surface layer. Eventually, the ice can no longer hold together under that stress, and it splits — forming a crevasse.

Think of it like pulling a piece of toffee apart. If you pull it slowly, it stretches and then cracks open. A glacier does the same thing, just over years or decades.

Crevasses also commonly form where a glacier flows over a bump, a ridge, or a steep drop in the terrain below it. The ice has to bend, and bending ice cracks.

One of the most chilling things about crevasses is that they can be invisible.

In many mountain and polar environments, snow falls on top of a glacier and builds up over the crevasses. This snow can harden and form a snow bridge — a thin arch of compacted snow that spans the crack like a lid on a box. From the surface, everything looks flat and solid. But beneath that innocent-looking white crust, there is a crevasse plunging deep into the ice.

People skiing, hiking, or climbing on glaciers can fall through a snow bridge without any warning. This is why mountaineers rope themselves together when crossing glaciers — if one person falls through into a crevasse, their teammates can stop them from falling all the way to the bottom and pull them out.

Crevasses vary enormously in size:

  • A small crevasse might be half a metre wide and a few metres deep — uncomfortable to fall into, but survivable and escapable.
  • A large crevasse can be several metres wide and drop 30 to 50 metres straight down — a fall into one of these, without a rope, would almost certainly be fatal.
  • At the bottom of a very deep crevasse, the pressure of all the ice above eventually squeezes the crack shut, so there is a maximum depth they reach — typically around 30–50 metres.

Crevasses are found in the most icy places on Earth:

  • Mountain glaciers — such as those in the Alps, the Himalayas, the Andes, and Alaska.
  • Polar ice sheets — the vast ice cover of Antarctica and Greenland is riddled with crevasses.
  • Ice falls — where a glacier flows steeply downhill, the ice tumbles and breaks into a chaotic jumble of crevasses and ice towers called seracs. The Khumbu Icefall on Mount Everest is one of the most famous and dangerous examples.
Crevasse vs. Crevice — Don't Confuse Them

These two words look and sound similar, and learners often mix them up.

CrevasseCrevice
What it cracksIce / glaciers onlyRock, walls, ground, or any hard surface
SizeLarge and deepUsually small and narrow
ContextMountaineering, glaciology, polar explorationEveryday use — e.g., a lizard hiding in a crevice

"She wedged her fingers into a crevice in the rock face to climb higher." ✅
"The mountaineer's foot broke through the snow bridge and she plunged into the crevasse." ✅
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

• The expedition team probed the snow ahead with long poles, searching for hidden crevasses before each step.
  • A network of crevasses made the final stretch of the glacier nearly impossible to cross.
  • He peered over the edge into the crevasse and could not see the bottom.
  • The crevasse had been bridged by snow all winter, but by spring the bridge had thinned dangerously.

A crevasse is a deep, often dangerous crack in a glacier or ice sheet, formed by the movement and stress of the flowing ice — and it is one of the most serious hazards that mountaineers and polar explorers face.
